title: Incorporating Societal Context
subtitle: Make the people, assumptions, and feedback around software visible
summary: A deployed system participates in a social environment that changes its behavior and is changed by it. Identifying agents, precepts, and artifacts makes people, beliefs, institutions, and infrastructure visible before they disappear inside a simplified technical model. Causal assumptions and feedback diagrams help teams discuss how an intervention might alter later inputs or outcomes. The health-care example shows why a convenient proxy can misrepresent the need the system is meant to address. The toxicity-classification case shows the value of examining data with specialists and responding constructively to criticism. A useful model remains open to revision as context changes.

concepts.title: Societal context
concepts.body: Societal context is a dynamic complex system surrounding software. It includes agents such as users and institutions, precepts or beliefs held by those agents, and artifacts such as laws, interfaces, datasets, and physical infrastructure.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A benefits portal depends on applicants’ access to documents, caseworkers’ practices, and local institutions. Its team studies those relationships instead of modeling eligibility as a form submission alone.

concepts.title: Agents, precepts, artifacts
concepts.body: Listing these three categories prevents an abstract model from erasing the people and institutions that shape outcomes. For SpeekSplendid, speech-impaired users, coaches, accessibility rules, microphones, language norms, and beliefs about “good” speech all matter.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: In a tutoring service, learners and teachers are agents, beliefs about acceptable language are precepts, and microphones and lesson materials are artifacts. Naming them exposes whose assumptions shape the product.

concepts.title: Explicit causality
concepts.body: Abstraction helps engineers reason about a system, but hidden assumptions can distort it. Writing causal assumptions explicitly makes a model discussable: a change in access may alter behavior, which changes data, which feeds a later decision.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A team writes down its assumption that adding appointment reminders will improve attendance, then checks whether unreliable transport could prevent that relationship from holding.

concepts.title: Causal loops
concepts.body: Causal loop diagrams show reinforcing and balancing feedback rather than only a one-way pipeline. They help teams seek other perspectives, choose subject-matter collaborators, benchmark assumptions, and identify where an intervention may create a new effect.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A recommendation system gives popular creators more exposure, producing more clicks that further increase their ranking. A causal loop makes this reinforcing effect visible before interpreting clicks as independent evidence of quality.

misconceptions.claim: Societal context is equivalent to ordinary functional correctness.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter separates this concern from “works as coded”: Societal context is a dynamic complex system surrounding software.

misconceptions.claim: A single review proves the product will remain responsible.
misconceptions.correction: Users, contexts, and dependencies change; feedback, monitoring, and revision are required.

scenario.title: Causal map for speech coaching
scenario.context: SpeekSplendid scores speech and suggests coaching. Engineers must choose whether to model users, institutions, beliefs, and artifacts explicitly before launch.

options.label: Build a causal loop with affected experts
options.benefit: Makes assumptions about coaching, language norms, and feedback discussable.
options.cost: Workshops take time and diagrams simplify a complex social system.
options.consequence: A speech-impaired participant identifies a harmful proxy, leading to a safer evaluation plan.

options.label: Model only the speech signal
options.benefit: Keeps the prototype small and technically legible.
options.cost: Social feedback and institutional context remain invisible.
options.consequence: The prototype rewards a narrow accent and the team later discovers the issue through user abandonment.

scenario.debrief: Both choices are defensible under different constraints; the responsible decision states the accepted consequence and the evidence that could change it.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of societal context?
quiz.explanation: The chapter defines agents, beliefs or precepts, and artifacts such as laws, interfaces, or infrastructure.

quiz.question: What does a causal loop diagram add?
options: It proves a prediction will occur.
It makes feedback assumptions and reinforcing or balancing effects discussable.
It removes the need for domain experts.
quiz.explanation: Diagrams expose assumptions and help teams seek other perspectives; they are not proof.

quiz.question: In the SpeekSplendid example, why identify speech-impaired users and language experts?
options: Their context can change what good speech and useful coaching mean.
They provide a replacement for all testing.
quiz.explanation: Different agents and expertise shape the system’s meaning and consequences.

exercise.title: Draw societal context
exercise.prompt: Create a causal map for a system.
